content:
On August 9 this year, the Hong Kong Observatory recorded its highest temperature of 36.9°C since records began in 1884, while Sheung Shui reached an even higher 39.8°C in the mid-afternoon. In the oppressive heat, I took shelter in a long, narrow apartment, leaving only a thin crack in the window for air. In extreme temperatures, hot air really does pour indoors, so I shut the balcony door and the living room windows tight. I live on a mid-floor flat sandwiched between two small hills, and except at noon, the sun is blocked from every side. Even without air conditioning, the three ceiling fans creak and spin out a breeze. In a Hong Kong-style heatwave, one must learn to be grateful.

In record-breaking heat, I stayed home to do laundry. After one in the afternoon, I washed two large bedsheets and duvet covers, four pairs of jeans, and a pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I turned the bedsheets and duvet covers inside out and hung them out again. By a little past six in the evening, I gathered the warm laundry in my arms—clothes so warm they felt as if they had just come out of a commercial tumble dryer at the laundromat. I laid them on the bed; I couldn't remember the last time in half a century that I had air-dried laundry smelling this clean. I should have been worrying about my friends under the scorching sun. The only way to offset the cruelty of the fierce sun, bit by bit, load by load, was to get the washing done.

August has become a torment. I don't know how many more rounds it will take to break free from this recurring summer farewell. In a dream one night, I was strutting proudly, walking arm-in-arm with my mother, telling her: 'My mummy dear.' I gripped her tightly, overjoyed. Then I saw a mysterious woman ahead, draped in a long, deep maroon cloak. Subconsciously I didn't want to see her face, but in the dream the camera kept zooming in on her. She was a strange woman I didn't recognize. When I woke, the smugness of my dream surfaced, and what I remembered was this: I had dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of August 10, 2020, our whole family sang hymns, kissed my mother's forehead, and said goodbye to her—a perfect full stop. But learning to let go is a lesson you never master in a lifetime. The unwillingness to part is a quiet wound. Six years on, there are still countless small regrets lurking in the details, and my mind replays over and over the days that led to that one day six years ago.

The regret and reluctance of parting can come at any age; it doesn't pick its time. A student in my writing class wrote about her late grandmother. It was a piece of recollection, mourning, and regret. When she was very little, she resented living with her grandmother in the countryside. During the day, with the boundless energy of a little imp, she bickered with her grandmother, who would pinch her ear; she would strike back, letting her grandmother feel the pain she had felt. Then, peeking through the crack in the door, the little girl saw her frail, elderly grandmother secretly wipe away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with a fever, and walked dazed to her grandmother's side, saying: 'I feel terrible.'

To feel terrible is to feel unwell—the way a child experiences illness. Burning up with a high fever, her grandmother, without a word, found fresh clothes and dressed her, then carried her on her back to the hospital to see a doctor. That medicinal oil smell she had once found so repulsive carried her, hazily, to the hospital. Before long, the smell faded somehow, and the little girl sat waiting alone near the reception desk. Then some adults asked her: 'Where is your family?' As she spoke, she began to cry, until the scent of the medicinal oil drifted close again, and she calmed down and waited quietly for the doctor to give her an injection and medicine.

Back home, the medicinal oil smell was as usual, but it had lost its sharp edge. From the kitchen came the rhythmic chopping of meat on the cutting board, and the warm fragrance of rice porridge rising from the pot. The essence of life is simple and clear, no explanation needed.

I wonder, who is the one cooking porridge today when I'm sick?

When I was little, it was usually dad, sometimes mum, who would patiently chop beef and make porridge for me. This was a sick-day menu, and I was the only one who got to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this special meat congee: 'I want beef porridge with scallions and vegetables.' That was a sick-day privilege. Now, no one makes this porridge for me anymore; when I fall ill, I will never taste that kind of beef porridge again.

'Now when you're sick, just order from Food Panda.' A friend suggested. Other friends cook plain porridge or fish congee for their wives. 'Sometimes I make minced pork porridge.' 'Hand-chopped, of course, not from a blender.' 'It only takes a few minutes to chop it.' A pot of porridge makes a person feel cherished.

'In your whole life, there aren't many people who will cook porridge for you when you're sick. When you grow up, the most likely scenario is that you are the one cooking for others. Many people have been through this. Whatever your feelings, say a proper goodbye, say what's in your heart. Readers will find comfort in it, too.' I told the student. She looked at me, a flicker of light in her eyes.

A piece about her grandmother can bring comfort. My father, my mother, my grandmother—these are the stories we can write naturally.

The student is more than just someone with good writing skills. She latched onto the medicinal oil as her anchor, and circling around it, conveyed the true feelings she had for her closest kin. She doesn't have to be the most devoted grandchild, but the time together that was ordained by fate now makes it impossible for her to forget all that her grandmother did for her, and impossible not to understand that people grow up in ways they cannot quite grasp. In the end, she handed in a piece that was profoundly moving and deeply 'uncomfortable' to read.

The medicinal oil went from being hated, to being dependable, to being shameful, to being an object of remembrance. It turns out that on the first day of primary school, the girl was teased by her classmates for smelling of medicinal oil—they called her a country bumpkin. She cried and ran home, and fiercely ordered her grandmother to scrub every single piece of clothing with heavy-handed amounts of washing powder. Her grandmother hugged the clothes and wept. From the time the girl was eight months old, her grandmother had raised her; but once the granddaughter grew up and went to school, stepping into the wider world, she became a different person, and wounded her grandmother's heart. After moving back to live with her mother, one day her grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The girl went back to visit with her mother, only to realise that she was no longer 'recognised'.

'You can't be my granddaughter. She doesn't like talking to me.' The old grandmother told the girl.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my mother? I don't think so. Or maybe I have—I can't say for certain, just like the student. Family members sometimes hurt each other. The point is, as we go on, do we come to understand love more deeply?
